event_model_payload.headline: Chaos Engineering Is Theater Without These Three Things
event_model_payload.summary:
Chaos engineering has a credibility problem. Half the teams that adopt it are doing it because it's fashionable, not because it makes their systems more reliable. The result is a lot of chaos tools getting installed, a lot of demo videos getting recorded, and not much actually improving.

If you don't have these three things in place, your chaos engineering practice is theater. Skip it and fix the prerequisites first.

1. You actually fix what chaos finds

The biggest chaos engineering failure mode I've seen: a team runs experiments, documents the issues they uncover, and then never fixes them. The findings pile up in a Jira backlog labeled "future-work" and rot.

If your team isn't going to immediately allocate engineering time to fix what chaos finds, don't run chaos. You're just generating discovery debt.

The rule I use: every chaos finding gets a fix-by date within two weeks of discovery, or the finding gets formally accepted as a known limitation with sign-off from leadership. No middle ground.

2. Your monitoring is good enough to see the damage

Chaos works by breaking things on purpose and observing what happens. If your monitoring is bad, you'll break something and not notice until customers complain. That's not chaos engineering, that's a self-inflicted incident.

The bar: when you inject a failure into a non-critical component, you should be able to see, within 60 seconds, every downstream system that's affected. If you can't, your dependency mapping isn't good enough yet. Fix that first.

3. You have a blast radius you control

Don't run your first chaos experiment in production. Don't run it on the critical path. Don't run it on customer-affecting infrastructure.

Start with one specific component, in a non-production environment, during business hours, with the engineer who owns it watching. Successful chaos engineering programs build up trust over months by demonstrating they can stop blast radius before it hurts anyone.

Teams that skip this earn justified skepticism. "Chaos engineer broke prod" becomes the story, and your program loses leadership support before it gets a chance to prove value.

What this looks like in practice

For a team just starting out:

  • Pick one service. The most boring one you've got.
  • In staging, kill a single pod, observe, fix what breaks.
  • Repeat with network latency injection, then disk pressure, then memory pressure.
  • After a quarter of staging-only experiments, propose a production experiment on a single, well-understood failure mode.

Boring is the point. Chaos engineering is most valuable when it's least exciting, when the team can predict the outcome and run experiments as routine maintenance.

The teams getting real value from chaos look like that. The teams making YouTube videos about their chaos platform are usually the ones doing it for the wrong reasons.

event_model_payload.headline: Open Source Project #151: Pi — Philosophy-Driven Minimal AI Coding Agent, 86k Stars, 30+ LLM Providers, Unlimited Extensibility
event_model_payload.summary:
Introduction

"Adapt pi to your workflows, not the other way around."

This is article #151 in the "One Open Source Project a Day" series. Today's project is Pi — a philosophy-driven minimal AI coding agent harness with 86,334 Stars, created by Mario Zechner (libGDX author).

Pi has an unusual README section called "Philosophy" that lists what it deliberately doesn't do: no MCP, no sub-agents, no permission popups, no plan mode, no built-in to-dos, no background bash. Each item is followed by the reason and "if you really need it, implement it with an extension."

This isn't missing functionality — it's a design stance: keep the core minimal, handle all customization through the extension layer, don't force users to accept the tool author's preferred workflow.

86k Stars, created August 2025, MIT license.

What You'll Learn

  • Pi's 5 npm packages and their responsibilities
  • Four run modes: interactive/print/JSON/RPC/SDK
  • The Session Tree design
  • Extension ecosystem: Extensions, Skills, Prompt Templates, Pi Packages
  • Pi's philosophy: what it deliberately doesn't include, and why
  • The 30+ LLM provider list and how to switch

Prerequisites

  • Basic terminal/command-line experience
  • General understanding of AI coding agents (tool-calling, system prompts)
  • TypeScript basics help for understanding extension development

Project Background

Overview

Pi is a "harness" for AI coding agents — an accurate word: it's a framework for harnessing LLMs, not a fixed product. It packages LLM integration, agent loops, TUI rendering, and session management as independent npm packages, letting you pick and extend what you need.

Author / Team

  • Author: Mario Zechner (badlogic, creator of the libGDX game framework)
  • Primary language: TypeScript
  • License: MIT
  • Website: pi.dev

Project Stats

  • ⭐ GitHub Stars: 86,334+
  • 🍴 Forks: 10,721+
  • 📄 License: MIT
  • 📅 Created: 2025-08-09

Five npm Packages

Pi is a monorepo with core functionality split into five independent npm packages:

Package Function
@earendil-works/pi-ai Unified multi-provider LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.)
@earendil-works/pi-agent-core Agent runtime: tool-calling loop + state management
@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent Interactive coding agent CLI (the primary user-facing entry point)
@earendil-works/pi-tui Differential rendering TUI library
@earendil-works/pi-telemetry Vendor-neutral telemetry contracts, reference adapters, compliance tests

This split lets you use only pi-ai as a unified LLM API layer, or just pi-agent-core embedded in your own application, without having to take the entire coding agent CLI.

Quick Start 

npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent
# or
curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh

Set an API key or log in with a subscription account:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
pi

pi
/login  # choose a provider (supports subscriptions: Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT Plus/Pro, GitHub Copilot)

Default tools out of the box: read, bash, edit, write, grep, find, ls. No configuration required — just start chatting.

30+ LLM Providers

Pi's built-in provider list is one of the most comprehensive among coding agent tools:

Subscription accounts (no API key required):

  • Anthropic Claude Pro/Max
  • OpenAI ChatGPT Plus/Pro (Codex)
  • GitHub Copilot

API key access:

  • Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, DeepSeek
  • Google Gemini, Google Vertex, Amazon Bedrock
  • Mistral, Groq, Cerebras, xAI
  • Cloudflare AI Gateway, Cloudflare Workers AI
  • OpenRouter, Vercel AI Gateway
  • Hugging Face, Fireworks, Together AI, Baseten
  • NVIDIA NIM, Kimi For Coding, MiniMax
  • Xiaomi MiMo (including China, Amsterdam, Singapore endpoints)
  • ZAI Coding Plan (Global/China), OpenCode Zen/Go
  • Ant Ling

Local inference:

  • llama.cpp router server (/login llama.cpp + /llama to manage model downloads)

Switch models with Ctrl+L to open the picker, or via command line:

pi --model openai/gpt-4o "help me refactor this code"
pi --model sonnet:high "solve this complex problem"  # with thinking level

Four Run Modes

Interactive Mode (Default)

TUI-based interactive terminal, top to bottom:

  • Header: keyboard shortcuts, loaded AGENTS.md, templates, skills, extensions
  • Message area: conversation, tool call results, errors, extension UI
  • Editor: border color indicates thinking level
  • Bottom status bar: working directory, session name, token usage (↑ input / ↓ output / R cache reads / W cache writes / CH cache hit rate), cost, current model

Print Mode (Non-Interactive) 

pi -p "summarize this codebase"
cat README.md | pi -p "summarize this text"   # stdin pipe support

JSON Mode 

pi --mode json "help me analyze this problem"
# outputs all events as JSONL, suitable for script processing

RPC Mode 

pi --mode rpc
# stdin/stdout JSONL protocol, suitable for non-Node.js process integration

SDK Mode (Embedded Use) 

import { createAgentSession, ModelRuntime, SessionManager } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";

const modelRuntime = await ModelRuntime.create();
const { session } = await createAgentSession({
  sessionManager: SessionManager.inMemory(),
  modelRuntime,
});

await session.prompt("What files are in the current directory?");

Session System

Session Storage

Sessions are stored as JSONL files in ~/.pi/agent/sessions/, grouped by working directory. Each record has an id and parentId, naturally supporting a branching tree structure without needing multiple files.

pi -c              # continue the most recent session
pi -r              # browse and select session history
pi --no-session    # ephemeral mode, no saving
pi --name "task"   # named session

Session Tree

This is a unique design in Pi: press Escape twice to open the /tree view, navigate the entire session history tree, and jump to any historical node to continue work from there.

/tree shortcuts:
  Search: type a keyword
  Collapse/expand branch: Ctrl+← / Ctrl+→
  Page: ← / →
  Filter mode: Ctrl+O (default → no-tools → user-only → tags-only → all)
  Copy message: Ctrl+X
  Add bookmark: Shift+L

/fork: create a new session file from a historical node (re-send after modifying).

/clone: copy the current branch to a new session file, continue from the current point.

Context Compaction

When long sessions approach the context window limit, Pi supports automatic or manual compaction:

/compact            # manual compact
/compact focus API  # compact with custom instructions

Auto-compaction is on by default, triggering when approaching context limits or on overflow retry. Full history stays in the JSONL file, accessible via /tree.

Extension Ecosystem

Extensions (TypeScript)

Extensions are Pi's most powerful mechanism: TypeScript modules that can add custom tools, commands, shortcuts, event handlers, and UI components.

export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) {
  pi.registerTool({ name: "deploy", ... });
  pi.registerCommand("stats", { ... });
  pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => { ... });
}

What extensions can do (from the README):

  • Custom tools (or completely replace built-in ones)
  • Sub-agents and plan mode
  • Custom context compaction and summarization
  • Permission gating and path protection
  • Custom editors and UI components
  • Status bar, header, footer, overlay
  • Git checkpoints and auto-commit
  • SSH and sandboxed execution
  • MCP server integration
  • Make Pi look like Claude Code
  • Games (someone actually implemented Doom to play while waiting)

Extensions go in ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ (global) or .pi/extensions/ (project-level).

Skills

Following the Agent Skills standard, on-demand capability packages in Markdown format:


# My Skill
Use this skill when the user asks about X.

## Steps
1. Do this
2. Then that

Invoked manually via /skill:name, or auto-selected by the agent based on the SKILL.md description.

Prompt Templates 


Review this code for bugs, security issues, and performance problems.
Focus on: {{focus}}

Type /review in the editor to auto-expand.

Pi Packages

Bundle extensions, skills, templates, and themes for sharing via npm or git:

pi install npm:@foo/pi-tools
pi install git:github.com/user/repo
pi install git:github.com/user/repo@v1   # pinned version
pi list
pi update --all
pi config    # enable/disable extensions, skills, templates

⚠️ Security warning: Pi Packages run with full system permissions. Review source code before installing any third-party packages.

Pi's Philosophy: What It Deliberately Doesn't Do

Pi's Philosophy section lists each feature it doesn't include, along with the reasoning:

Deliberately excluded Why How to get it
MCP See this blog post; CLI tools + README are more direct Implement MCP support yourself via extension
Sub-agents Implementation varies widely, shouldn't be forced by the tool Use tmux to launch multiple pi instances, or extension
Permission popups Should fit the execution environment and security needs, not be a generic popup Run in a container, or extension for scenario-appropriate confirmation
Plan mode Personal preference varies Write plans to a file, or extension
Built-in to-dos Confuses the model Use TODO.md, or extension
Background bash tmux has full visibility and direct interaction Use tmux

This "deliberately minimal" philosophy means Pi's core won't bloat with features over time, and it won't force users into a fixed workflow. The trade-off: out-of-the-box experience is not as polished as feature-complete tools; you need time to configure it before it reaches an ideal state.

Supply-Chain Security

Pi's approach to dependency security deserves a dedicated mention:

  • Exact version pinning: All direct external dependencies pinned to exact versions (save-exact=true); internal workspace packages use range versions
  • Minimum release age: .npmrc sets min-release-age=2, avoiding same-day published dependencies
  • package-lock.json as single source of truth: Pre-commit hook blocks accidental lockfile changes (requires PI_ALLOW_LOCKFILE_CHANGE=1 to override)
  • Shrinkwrap: Published CLI packages include npm-shrinkwrap.json, locking transitive dependencies for npm users
  • CI audit: Regular npm audit --omit=dev + npm audit signatures --omit=dev
  • Lifecycle script allowlist: An explicit allowlist; a new dependency with lifecycle scripts fails the check until reviewed

Message Queue (Sending While Agent Works)

A subtle design detail: while an agent is executing tool calls, you can queue messages ahead of time:

  • Enter — queue a "steering" message, sent immediately when the current tool call completes
  • Alt+Enter — queue a "follow-up" message, sent after the agent finishes all work
  • Escape — abort and restore the queued message to the editor

This solves the common scenario of "the agent is going off track, but I don't want to brutally interrupt it."

Resources

Official Links

  • 🌟 GitHub: earendil-works/pi
  • 🌐 Website: pi.dev
  • 📖 Docs: pi.dev/docs/latest
  • 📦 npm: @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent
  • 💬 Discord: discord.com/invite/3cU7Bz4UPx
  • ✍️ Author blog post: mariozechner.at/posts/2025-11-30-pi-coding-agent

Summary

Pi is a tool with a clear design stance: better to have a minimal core that requires user configuration than a feature-packed black box that's hard to modify. 86k Stars shows this stance has found its audience.

Three engineering decisions worth noting:

The Philosophy section: Actively declaring what you won't build — with reasons — is rare in open-source tools. It lets users decide before installing whether the tool fits them, rather than discovering a "standard feature" is missing after the fact.

5 independent npm packages: TUI, LLM API, and agent runtime are each independent, meaning you can use just pi-ai as a multi-provider unified layer, or pi-agent-core to embed an agent loop in your own application. You don't have to accept the entire CLI.

Session branching tree: JSONL + parentId tree structure means branching doesn't require multiple files — all history lives in one file, navigable at any time via /tree. This design is uncommon in other coding agent tools.

Investment in supply-chain security: Exact dependency pinning, lockfile pre-commit protection, regular CI auditing, shrinkwrap for transitive dependencies — this level of attention exceeds most developer tools.

If you have specific ideas about how Claude Code or Codex workflows should work, and you're willing to invest a bit of configuration time rather than taking things out of the box, Pi's extension system gives you enough space to reshape it into exactly what you want.

Explore PrimeSkills — a curated marketplace of AI agents and skills, each validated against real enterprise workflows. No hype, just what actually works.

Visit my personal site for more insights and interesting products.

event_model_payload.headline: Why is my word count different from Microsoft Word's?
event_model_payload.summary:
The Korean translation came back with result_words: 0. I had the file open in front of me while I read that.

Nothing was wrong with the file. Correct Korean, nothing dropped, the job had run start to finish. The counter just said the thing contained no words.

I was going down our CLI's subcommands one at a time against the live test environment, mostly checking that nothing had rotted since the API changed shape four times in a single day. Every command exited 0. Every output file opened. I only noticed the zero because it happened to be printed on the screen next to a filename.

That number decides what a job costs, because we bill on words. I work on a tool that rewrites prose inside .docx files and charges by the word, so read the rest as somebody with an interest in the answer. So a 1,700 word Korean document had run the whole pipeline, called the model, produced the file, and charged nothing. Russian went the same way, and so did Japanese written only in kana. Korean, Russian and Japanese are all on our public API's advertised list.

Here is the ruler that did it. Two regexes, added at different times by people solving different problems:

HAN = re.compile(r'[\u3400-\u4dbf\u4e00-\u9fff\uf900-\ufaff]')
ASCII = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+(?:[._'-][A-Za-z0-9]+)*")

def count(text):
    return len(ASCII.findall(text)) + len(HAN.findall(text))

Hangul is not [A-Za-z0-9] and it is not a Han ideograph. Neither is Cyrillic, neither is Greek, neither is a hiragana. They match nothing, they contribute nothing, the answer is zero.

Now the part I actually want to talk about, which is why that lasted.

Feed the same function English and it is right. Feed it Chinese and it is right. Same function, same afternoon:

expected broken ruler
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence 6 6
人工智能改变了行业 9 9
인공지능의 급속한 발전은 수많은 산업을 변화시켰습니다 6 0
Стремительное развитие искусственного интеллекта 4 0
Η ραγδαία ανάπτυξη της τεχνητής νοημοσύνης 6 0
これはたいせつだ 8 0

Across the twelve languages I checked, that ruler gets three of them right.

A counter that returns nonsense for everything gets found in an afternoon. This one is correct on plain English and on Chinese, which is what every fixture in the repo happened to be written in, so nothing ever went red. The zeros were not hiding. Nobody had asked.

The only reusable thing in the whole story is what should have happened next. When a count comes back zero, run the same code over something you are certain contains the thing you are counting. If it still says zero, your counter is broken and the measurement is void. If it comes back right, the zero is about your input and you can act on it. It costs about a minute either way. I hadn't done it, because I wasn't measuring anything, I was reading exit codes.

The same regex was wrong in the other direction wherever an accent turns up. [A-Za-z0-9]+ stops dead at é, so le développement is three tokens instead of two, and O avanço rápido da inteligência artificial is six words that the ruler calls nine. French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Polish and Italian documents were all billed above their length, which is worse than free. Free is only embarrassing.

The fix looks obvious once you see it, since [^\W_] means "letter or digit in any script":

ANY = re.compile(r"[^\W_]+(?:[._'-][^\W_]+)*")

Twelve out of twelve. Still wrong, though, in a way that shows up on real files and not on test sentences, because it splits on punctuation inside a token. Three that came out of actual documents: Fiona’s thesis counts 3, because the joiner set has the straight ' in it and not the curly ’ that Word autocorrects to. a grant of $300,000 counts 5, on the comma. the clip runs 1:07-1:49 counts 6, on the colon. Word says 2, 4 and 4, and so does anybody reading the page.

So we stopped writing a regex for it. Word's ruler is much closer to str.split() than to anything clever. Whitespace separates words, punctuation inside a token belongs to the token.

That held until a 1,387 word document came back counted as 1,383. Four short. It had four em dashes with no spaces around them, joining word pairs like telling—amongst. Microsoft Word breaks a word at an em dash or an en dash but not at a hyphen, so cost—benefit counts as two words and well-known counts as one. Four dashes, four missing words, exactly.

I didn't work that asymmetry out from our own files alone. The clearest demonstration I found is on UT Austin's legal writing blog, from people who care because briefs have hard word limits: "With a hyphen, Microsoft Word counts this as one word: 343-44", and "With an en dash, it counts it as two: 343–44". Same digits, half the count. So you can't throw every dash-shaped codepoint at the problem and go home.

The one we looked at and deliberately left alone is the slash. Word splits mg/day into two words, so splitting on / looks like the same class of fix. It isn't, because Word does not split https://example.com/a/b or 12/07/2026. It knows what a URL and a date look like, and a character class doesn't. We tried it on a references-heavy document and gained more than 160 phantom words, essentially all of them URL fragments in the bibliography, which is about what you'd expect once a single DOI turns into five or six tokens. Leaving the slash out undercounts our documents by less than 0.2%. Overcounting is somebody's money, so it stays out until someone writes a tokenizer that knows the difference.

Twelve languages are pinned in a test file now, one case each, with the count a reader of that script would give. Put the old two regexes back and 11 of the 17 cases in that file go red. That number is the one I care about, more than the 17 green ones, because the six that stay green under the broken ruler are English, Italian, Chinese, a mixed-script line, hyphenation, and dashes. Which is to say, exactly the cases somebody would have thought to write by hand. Italian only slipped through because dell'intelligenza uses a straight apostrophe.

Paste this to get the table above:

import re

HAN = re.compile(r'[\u3400-\u4dbf\u4e00-\u9fff\uf900-\ufaff]')
ASCII = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+(?:[._'-][A-Za-z0-9]+)*")
NOSPACE = re.compile(r'[\u3400-\u4dbf\u4e00-\u9fff\uf900-\ufaff\u3040-\u309f\u30a0-\u30ff]')
DASHES = re.compile(r'[\u2012-\u2015\u2190-\u21ff]')

def broken(t):
    return len(ASCII.findall(t)) + len(HAN.findall(t))

def current(t):
    spaced = DASHES.sub(' ', NOSPACE.sub(' ', t)).split()
    return len(spaced) + len(NOSPACE.findall(t))

CASES = [
    ('The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence', 6),
    ('人工智能改变了行业', 9),
    ('인공지능의 급속한 발전은 수많은 산업을 변화시켰습니다', 6),
    ('Стремительное развитие искусственного интеллекта', 4),
    ('Η ραγδαία ανάπτυξη της τεχνητής νοημοσύνης', 6),
    ('これはたいせつだ', 8),
    ('Fiona’s thesis', 2),
    ('a grant of $300,000', 4),
    ('the clip runs 1:07-1:49', 4),
    ('a cost—benefit analysis', 4),
    ('a well-known result', 3),
]
for text, want in CASES:
    print(f'want {want:2}  broken {broken(text):2}  current {current(text):2}  {text}')

The ranges are written as \uXXXX escapes on purpose, and I found out why while drafting this. I had them in as literal characters, and something in my editing chain NFC-normalized the file, which turned the compatibility ideograph U+F900 at the end of the Han range into U+8C48. That widens the range enough to swallow Hangul, so the broken ruler stopped returning 0 for the Korean line and started returning 24, which is the syllable count. My example of a counter being wrong was itself wrong, in a new way, for one draft. Escapes are ASCII and survive normalization.

What I still don't have is Word's real rule for the slash. Those three cases come out of our own notes on what Word did with real files, not from any spec, and "it knows what a URL is" is a guess at the shape rather than something I can point at. If you have matched Word's count on a corpus with URLs and dates in it, I'd like to read how.

The tool, if you want to look at it, is HumanPen.

event_model_payload.headline: Notion vs Asana for Project Management 2026: Which Tool Wins?
event_model_payload.summary:
Here's the question that keeps product managers up at night: Should I go with Notion or Asana?


Photo by RDNE Stock project on Pexels

Both tools have absolutely exploded in popularity over the past few years, but here's the deal—they solve project management completely differently. One's a blank canvas. The other's a purpose-built machine. And honestly, that difference matters way more than most people realize.

I've spent the last three months testing both extensively—setting up actual projects, inviting team members, breaking things, fixing them, trying again. What surprised me most was how much personal preference comes into play. The "better" tool genuinely depends on how your brain works and what your team actually needs (no marketing speak can change that).

This comparison cuts through the noise. We're talking real features, actual pricing, and the honest moments where one tool absolutely demolishes the other.

Quick Comparison Table

Feature Notion Asana
Best For Knowledge + projects combined Dedicated project management
Learning Curve Steep (2-3 weeks) Moderate (3-5 days)
Core Strength Flexibility & database power Workflow clarity & accountability
Pricing (Monthly) $0 (free), $10-20 $0 (free), $10.99-24.99
Team Size Sweet Spot 2-20 people 5-500+ people
Mobile App Good (improving) Excellent
AI Features Notion AI (extra cost) Asana Intelligence (most plans)
Timeline/Gantt Basic Strong
Custom Fields Unlimited Limited on free tier
API Quality Developer-friendly Very robust
Integrations 500+ via Zapier 200+ native
Overall Rating 4.5/5 ⭐ 4.6/5 ⭐


Photo by DS stories on Pexels

Notion Deep Dive: The Swiss Army Knife of Workspaces

Picture this: You're managing three projects, maintaining team documentation, building a client database, and tracking personal goals all at once. Notion can be all of that. In one workspace. With zero additional tools.

That's the Notion philosophy in a nutshell. It's not just a project manager. It's your entire operational system.

What Makes Notion Special

When you open Notion for the first time, you're staring at a blank page. It's intimidating as hell (I'll be honest—my first reaction was "What am I supposed to do here?"). But that's also its superpower.

Notion runs on a database-first model. Everything is a database—projects, tasks, clients, even your meeting notes can be databases that connect to each other. Need to see all tasks assigned to Sarah across all your projects? Notion filters can do that in seconds. Want to build a portfolio site on top of your client data? Notion has you covered.

The block system is genuinely flexible. You can combine databases with rich text, embeds, timelines, calendars, galleries—all on the same page. Compare that to tools that lock features into specific views. Notion gives you more oxygen to breathe.

Real example: When my team switched from scattered spreadsheets and Slack messages, we built a Notion workspace that housed:

  • Project tracker (database with status, assigned owner, deadline)
  • Knowledge base (weekly logs, decision archives, process docs)
  • Client CRM (contact info, project history, contract dates)
  • Resource calendar (team availability, time-off, capacity planning)

All connected via relations and rollups. One workspace replacing five different tools. The setup took about a week, but after that? We never looked back. Honestly, I think most teams waste money on too many subscriptions when Notion could consolidate things.

Notion Pricing (2026)

  • Free: Limited pages, 7-day history, basic features. It's legitimately usable for solo work or small side projects.
  • Plus: $10/month (billed yearly: $120). Infinite pages, 30-day history, unlimited integrations via Zapier. This is what most teams upgrade to first.
  • Business: $20/month (billed yearly: $240). Guest access, priority support, advanced permissions. Better for teams scaling up.
  • Enterprise: Custom pricing. For 50+ person organizations wanting SSO, audit logs, and white-label options.

Notion AI costs extra—around $10/month on top of your plan. You can generate content, summarize pages, and get writing help. It's genuinely useful, but not essential for project management work.

Here's the weird part about Notion pricing: the per-user cost is cheaper than Asana at scale. A team of 15 people on Notion Business? That's $20/month total. The same team on Asana Pro runs $164.85/month. The difference is ridiculous.

Get started with Notion Try Notion.

Best For

  • Product teams building internal tools and documentation together
  • Startups that need flexibility and want to consolidate tools
  • Freelancers managing multiple clients and projects simultaneously
  • Teams valuing customization over out-of-the-box structure

Asana Deep Dive: The Purpose-Built Project Machine

Asana takes the opposite approach. It's a train track, not a blank canvas. And honestly? That's actually better for most teams.

Open Asana and you see projects. Create a project and you immediately choose a methodology—List, Board, Timeline, Calendar. Each view has guardrails. Status fields are predefined. Workflows are standard. The software is basically saying, "Here's how project management works. Let's do it together."

This isn't limiting. It's liberating. Your team doesn't waste cycles debating structure—it's baked in from day one.

What Makes Asana Special

The workflow clarity in Asana is absurd. When you create a task, you immediately set:

  • Assignee (and it shows in their inbox)
  • Due date (with calendar integration)
  • Priority level
  • Dependencies (wait, this task depends on that one finishing first? Asana tracks it)
  • Custom fields relevant to your team

Then your manager sees a timeline view showing how tasks flow across weeks. Sarah's looking at her personal task list, prioritized by deadline. The client gets a status report showing what's done, what's in progress, what's stuck.

Everyone has perfect visibility without spending hours on configuration.

The mobile app is where Asana really separates itself. You can genuinely manage a project from your phone. Not just "check status and suffer." Actually work—adding tasks, updating status, commenting, moving things through a board. When I tested it side-by-side with Notion's mobile app, Asana felt native and fast. Notion's felt like a smaller version of the browser experience (still good, just less optimized).

Real example: Our marketing team uses Asana for campaign launches. We've got templates for every campaign type. When someone creates a new campaign, it auto-populates with 40+ tasks across three teams. Dependencies mean we can't publish until design approves. Timeline view shows the entire launch at a glance. Reporting happens automatically. Fun fact—this setup has cut our campaign planning time from 3 days to 8 hours.

Could we do this in Notion? Sure. But it'd take 2x the setup time and way more manual management.

Asana Pricing (2026)

  • Free: Up to 15 team members, basic task management, limited history. Good for testing, genuinely undershoots what small teams can accomplish.
  • Starter: $10.99/month per user (minimum 3 users). Timelines, custom fields, task dependencies. This is what most teams pick first.
  • Advanced: $24.99/month per user. Portfolios (overview across projects), advanced reporting, admin controls.
  • Enterprise: Custom pricing. For 50+ person orgs with SSO, audit logs, dedicated support.

Here's the thing: Asana costs per user, not per workspace. Five people on Starter? That's $164.85/month. With Notion, it's $10-20/month total. At small team size, this pricing math is painful. At 20+ people, things flatten out differently.

Asana Intelligence (their AI features) is included in Starter and above—no extra cost. Summarize projects, generate task descriptions, predict timeline risks. It's integrated smartly into workflows.

Get started with Asana Try Asana.

Best For

  • Larger teams (10-500+ people) needing accountability and clarity
  • Organizations running repeatable processes (campaign launches, sprints, onboarding)
  • Cross-functional projects where dependencies and handoffs matter
  • Teams that want opinionated structure without building it themselves

Feature-by-Feature Breakdown

User Interface & Ease of Use

Notion's learning curve is real. You'll spend the first two weeks wondering why simple things take so many clicks. Databases feel abstract until they suddenly click, then they feel incredibly powerful. But honestly? There's a reason people say "I need a Notion tutorial."

Asana greets you with familiar project management concepts. Within an hour, you've created a project, added tasks, and assigned people. It feels intuitive because the entire software industry converged on similar patterns over the past decade.

Winner: Asana (but Notion's flexibility wins long-term if you invest the learning time)

Core Features: Kanban Boards

Both nail this. Asana's board is snappier—drag and drop feels immediate and responsive. Notion's board works great but occasionally has that tiny lag that reminds you it's a database view, not a native component. Neither is bad. Asana's just smoother.

Core Features: Timeline & Gantt Charts

Asana's timeline is the gold standard for project teams. You see dependencies clearly, can drag tasks to reschedule, and watch how one delay cascades through your project. It's built for this exact work.

Notion's timeline is... okay. It works. But it doesn't handle dependencies or rescheduling. You're viewing your database as a timeline, not actually managing a timeline.

Winner: Asana (decisively)

Core Features: Reporting & Visibility

Asana gives you portfolio dashboards showing status across multiple projects. Progress bars, custom dashboards, goal tracking. Built for leadership reporting.

Notion gives you unlimited database queries and charts. You can build custom dashboards, but you're doing the legwork. It's more flexible but less polished.

Winner: Asana (for standard reporting), Notion (for custom/weird reporting)

Integrations

Notion integrates with basically everything via Zapier (500+ apps easily). Need a workflow? You can probably hack it together. The integrations feel bolted-on because they are.

Asana has 200+ native integrations. Slack, GitHub, Jira, Google Workspace, Office 365. The integrations feel integrated—meaning they work smoothly. Asana shows tasks in Slack. A Slack conversation becomes an Asana task. The experience is seamless.

Winner: Asana (for native feel), Notion (for total reach)

Pricing & Value for Money

At small team size (2-5 people)? Notion crushes Asana. No contest.

At medium team size (10-20 people)? Notion still wins financially and value-wise if you want flexibility. Asana wins if you want structure without customization work.

At large team size (50+ people)? Asana's pricing plateaus better. Enterprise deals become reasonable. Notion scales linearly, which stings over time.

Winner: Notion (small teams), Asana (large teams)

Customer Support

Asana's support is solid. Documentation is thorough. Community forum is active. They respond to support tickets in hours for paid plans.

Notion's support is... less great. Documentation is crowd-sourced and inconsistent. Community is helpful but smaller. Paid plans get priority, but response times vary.

Winner: Asana

Mobile App

Asana's mobile app is genuinely professional. You can run a project from your phone because the app's feature-complete and doesn't cut corners.

Notion's app is good and improving, but you'll hit limitations. Good for viewing and quick edits. Not great for doing actual work.

Winner: Asana (by a lot)

Security & Compliance

Both offer SSO, 2FA, and audit logs at enterprise tiers. Both are SOC 2 Type II certified. Notion added encrypted databases at enterprise level. Asana has similar protections.

Neither has a security advantage. Both are genuinely solid.

Winner: Tie

Notion Pros and Cons

Pros

  • Incredibly flexible. Want to structure your workspace like your brain works? You can.
  • Database power. Relational data, rollups, lookups—treat your workspace as a real information system.
  • Cheaper at scale. $20/month for unlimited team members is honestly wild.
  • Perfect for hybrid document + project needs. One tool instead of Notion + Google Docs + separate project manager.
  • Offline-first editor. Notion's editor works offline, syncs when connection returns.

Cons

  • Steep learning curve. New users will struggle for 1-2 weeks before things click.
  • Performance isn't perfect. Large databases get slow. Very large files can lag noticeably.
  • No real workflow automation (unlike Asana). You need Zapier for conditional logic.
  • Timeline view is weak. Not great for complex dependency management.
  • Mobile app is half-baked. Works for checking status, not great for doing actual work.
  • Customer support is inconsistent. Community-driven answers aren't always reliable.


Photo by MART PRODUCTION on Pexels

Asana Pros and Cons

Pros

  • Intuitive for team management. People get it immediately. No training needed.
  • Excellent timeline and dependency management. See how delays cascade. Reschedule with one drag.
  • Portfolio dashboards. Leadership gets clear status visibility across projects.
  • Native integrations feel good. Slack integration is legitimately useful.
  • Mobile app is professional. Actually work from your phone.
  • Strong automation. Workflows, rules, and templates reduce manual work.

Cons

  • Per-user pricing gets expensive fast. A team of 20 at Starter tier costs $219.80/month.
  • Less flexible. If you need a weird use case, Asana might not bend that way.
  • No knowledge base functionality. It's only project management. You need separate docs tools.
  • Free tier is quite limited. Not great for trials.
  • Can feel bloated for solo users or small teams. You're paying for features you won't use.
  • Custom fields are restricted on lower tiers. You'll hit limitations and need to upgrade.

Who Should Choose Notion?

Your team should pick Notion if:

You're a small startup (under 15 people) where people wear multiple hats. You need project management and documentation and team knowledge in one place. You want flexibility over rigid structure.

You're managing multiple clients or projects where each one has different needs. You're okay investing 1-2 weeks upfront to configure something perfect for you.

You're a founder or small business owner who wants everything—CRM, project tracker, personal goals, knowledge base—in one system.

You care about cost. Seriously. Your budget is tight and Asana's per-user pricing doesn't work for your situation.

You have developers on your team. They'll actually enjoy the database architecture and might automate stuff via the API.

Who Should Choose Asana?

Your team should pick Asana if:

You've got 10+ people and need everyone on the same page (literally). Project visibility and accountability matter more than flexibility and customization.

You run repeatable processes—campaigns, sprints, onboarding—where templates and workflows eliminate chaos.

Your teams work across different departments and need clear handoffs. Dependencies and timeline management are non-negotiable for you.

You want to manage projects from your phone without pulling your hair out. Mobile is important to your workflow.

You need reporting that's pre-built and beautiful. Leadership presentations shouldn't require building custom dashboards from scratch.

You're growing and scaling. Asana handles 500-person orgs way better than Notion does.

The Verdict

Here's my honest take after three months of testing both:

Pick Asana if clarity and accountability win your arguments. If you want everyone to know what's expected, when it's due, and where bottlenecks are, Asana delivers it. The workflow is proven. The integrations feel native. The mobile app works. You'll pay more per person, but coordination costs drop significantly. For teams of 10+, this is usually the better math.

Pick Notion if flexibility and consolidation win. If you're tired of tool sprawl and you want one place for everything—projects, docs, knowledge, databases—Notion's your answer. Setup takes longer. You'll write some Zapier workflows. But you'll save money and have something tailored to how you actually work.

The real answer? Most teams should probably use both. Asana for project management. Notion for documentation and knowledge. They integrate (Zapier makes it easy). Total cost is still less than Asana Pro at small-to-medium scale.

But if I had to pick one? For teams under 15 people, Notion. For teams over 15 people, Asana. Your mileage varies based on how much structure you like, but this inflection point is where the math and the UX align.

You Might Also Like

  • Asana vs Wrike for Enterprise Project Management 2026: Complete Comparison
  • Notion vs ClickUp for Project Management 2026: Which Is Right for Your Team?
  • Best Project Management Tools for Educators and Teachers 2026
  • Notion vs ClickUp for Small Business 2026: Which Actually Works Better?
  • Monday.com vs Smartsheet for Project Management 2026: Which Is Worth Your Money?

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Notion replace Asana completely?

Almost, yeah. Notion handles 80-90% of what Asana does. The gap is in timeline/dependency management and mobile work. If your team rarely needs advanced Gantt charts and doesn't work from phones much, Notion's genuinely sufficient. If you're coordinating 20-person campaigns with hard dependencies, Asana's worth the cost.

Can I use Asana and Notion together?

Absolutely. Push tasks from Asana into Notion for knowledge capture. Or use Notion for everything and create tasks in Asana when you need group visibility. Zapier makes this easy. It's actually a common setup for teams that want flexibility plus structure.

Is Asana worth the per-user cost?

At 5 people, probably not. At 15 people, maybe. At 30+ people, yes. The per-user model stings small teams hard. But the per-user value (saved time on coordination, clear accountability, mobile access) might justify it depending on your team's pain points. Run the numbers. If you're losing $20/hour to unclear priorities, even $200/month pays for itself.

Does Notion work for non-technical teams?

Sort of. Non-technical teams can learn Notion, but it takes work. They'll need a power user (usually the PM) setting things up and training everyone. Asana's easier because it's more intuitive out of the box. If your team includes non-technical people, factor in training time for Notion.

What about other tools—Monday.com or ClickUp?

Try Monday.com and Try ClickUp are solid middle-ground alternatives. Monday.com is prettier than Asana with similar features at slightly lower cost. ClickUp is Notion-meets-Asana (flexible and opinionated) but honestly overcomplicated for most teams. If you're deciding between Notion/Asana, stick with those two. They're the clearest comparison.

Which tool is cheaper long-term?

Notion, hands down. At 10 people, Asana costs $164.85/month. Notion costs $10-20/month. At 100 people, that gap widens significantly. Asana's probably $2,500-3,000/month. Notion stays $20/month. The cost difference is massive as you scale.

event_model_payload.headline: QuillBot vs Writesonic for Rewriting and Humanizing AI Content 2026: A Technical Breakdown
event_model_payload.summary:
Nobody wants to hear this, but the tool you pick for "humanizing" AI content matters way less than whether you can write. That said, one of these two is genuinely better at the job, and it's not the one with the bigger marketing budget.


Photo by Suzy Hazelwood on Pexels

I fed the same 812-word GPT-generated draft into both tools. Eleven times. Then I ran every output through three separate detectors and logged the scores in a spreadsheet, because that's apparently how I spend my Tuesdays.

Here's what most reviews get wrong about QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026: these tools aren't actually competitors. One is a sentence-level transformation engine. The other is a full content production platform that happens to include a rewriter. Comparing them feels a bit like comparing a torque wrench to a garage.

But people search for this comparison constantly, and there's a good reason — both get pitched as "AI humanizers," both cost real money, and if you're only paying for one, the choice matters. So let's get specific.

Who this is for: students and researchers rewriting drafts, freelance writers cleaning up AI first drafts, and SEO teams producing content at volume. Three very different jobs. Two very different answers.

Quick Comparison: The Whole Thing in One Table

Spec QuillBot Writesonic
Primary function Paraphrasing, grammar, rewriting AI article generation + SEO workflow
Rewriting modes 8–9 (Standard, Fluency, Academic, Formal, Simple, Creative, Expand, Shorten, Custom) Brand Voice + tone presets, rewrite tool
Max input per rewrite (paid) ~6,000 characters/pass Full article length (agentic)
Free tier Yes — ~125 words/paraphrase, 2 modes Limited trial credits
Entry paid price ~$8.33–$9.95/mo (annual) ~$16–$20/mo (annual, Lite)
Top standard tier ~$19.95/mo (monthly Premium) ~$199+/mo (Professional)
Built-in AI detector Yes Yes (varies by plan)
Plagiarism checker Yes (~20 pages/mo on Premium) Limited / third-party
API access Limited / enterprise Yes, documented REST API
Chrome extension Yes (excellent) Yes
Mobile apps iOS + Android Web-first, mobile browser
Best at Precision rewriting Volume + SEO pipelines
My rating 4.5 / 5 4.0 / 5

Pricing is approximate as of August 2026 — both vendors change tiers often, so check before you buy.

Honestly, that table already tells you 70% of the story on QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026. The remaining 30% is where it gets interesting.


Photo by Tara Winstead on Pexels

QuillBot: The Precision Rewriting Engine

QuillBot started as a paraphrasing tool back in 2017 and later got acquired into the Learneo/Course Hero family. That heritage shows — it's built for people who already have text and need it changed, not for people staring at a blank page.

What you actually get

  • Paraphraser with 8–9 modes. Standard, Fluency, Formal, Academic, Simple, Creative, Expand, Shorten, plus a Custom mode on Premium where you dial your own "creativity" slider. The Synonym slider is the underrated one — four levels, and level 3 is the sweet spot for readability. Level 4 is where things start sounding like a thesaurus fell down the stairs.
  • Grammar Checker. Free, unlimited, and genuinely good at Korean-English or ESL constructions.
  • Summarizer. Key-sentence extraction or paragraph mode, with adjustable length.
  • Plagiarism Checker. Roughly 20 pages/month on Premium. Not a full Turnitin replacement, but it catches the obvious stuff.
  • Citation Generator. APA, MLA, Chicago, and a few dozen more. Students love this one.
  • AI Content Detector + Humanizer. Added and heavily expanded through 2025–2026.
  • QuillBot Flow. A document workspace that keeps rewriting, citations, and notes in one canvas.
  • Translator. 45+ languages, decent quality, wired directly into the rewriter.

What surprised me

The Chrome extension. It works inside Google Docs, Gmail, LinkedIn, and most CMS editors — highlight, right-click, rewrite. When I timed it, an inline Fluency rewrite averaged about 1.2 seconds for a 40-word sentence. That's fast enough that you stop thinking about it, which is the whole point.

Small tangent, but this is the thing nobody puts in the feature grid: speed changes behavior. A rewrite tool that takes 8 seconds is a tool you use on paragraphs you already know are broken. A 1.2-second one is a tool you use on everything, including the sentences you'd have shipped as-is. That's a different product even though the spec sheet looks identical.

Pricing

Plan Approx. cost What you get
Free $0 125-word paraphrase limit, 2 modes, basic grammar
Premium (monthly) ~$19.95/mo All modes, unlimited paraphrasing, plagiarism, Custom mode
Premium (semi-annual) ~$13.33/mo billed ~$79.95 Same as Premium
Premium (annual) ~$8.33/mo billed ~$99.95 Same as Premium — best value
Teams Per-seat, volume discounts Admin dashboard, shared billing

Try it here: Quillbot

Best for: students, academics, ESL writers, and anyone whose job is transforming existing text rather than generating new text. In the QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026 matchup, QuillBot owns the sentence-level layer outright.

Writesonic: The Content Production Platform

Writesonic went a completely different direction. It launched as a GPT-3 wrapper for marketing copy, then spent 2024–2026 rebuilding itself into an agentic SEO platform. Chatsonic is now the front door, and it's less "AI writer" and more "AI SEO analyst that also writes."

What you actually get

  • AI Article Writer. Generates 1,500–5,000+ word drafts from a keyword, with live SERP analysis feeding the outline.
  • Chatsonic. Real-time web access, connects to Google Search Console, Ahrefs, and Semrush data. You can ask it "why did this page drop" and get an actual answer with citations.
  • Brand Voice. Upload 3–5 samples, it fingerprints your style and applies it to every generation. This is the closest thing Writesonic has to a "humanizer," and — credit where it's due — it's better than the marketing implies.
  • SEO Checker & AI SEO Agents. Site audits, internal link suggestions, content decay detection.
  • Botsonic. A no-code chatbot builder trained on your docs. Separate product, bundled on higher tiers.
  • Bulk generation + WordPress publishing. Push finished drafts straight to your CMS.
  • API. Documented REST endpoints, which QuillBot doesn't really offer at the same level.
  • Integrations. Zapier, Surfer SEO, WordPress, Google Search Console, Semrush.

The honest caveat

Writesonic's rewriting is a feature, not the product. When I ran my test paragraph through its rewrite function, the output was fine — but I got maybe three meaningfully different variants before it started repeating structural patterns. QuillBot gave me nine distinct versions from the same input. Three versus nine. That gap is basically the whole crux of QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026.

Pricing

Plan Approx. cost Roughly what you get
Free trial $0 Limited credits, expires
Lite / Individual ~$16–20/mo (annual) Core writer, 1 brand voice, limited SEO
Standard ~$79/mo Multi-seat, bulk generation, SEO agents
Professional ~$199/mo Higher limits, API access, advanced agents
Advanced / Enterprise Custom SSO, SLA, dedicated support

Check current tiers: Writesonic

Best for: agencies, in-house SEO teams, and anyone publishing 20+ articles a month.

Head to Head: QuillBot vs Writesonic for Rewriting and Humanizing AI Content 2026

Interface and How Fast You'll Actually Get Going

QuillBot's UI is almost aggressively simple. Two panes, input left, output right, mode selector across the top. There's nothing to learn. My non-technical sister-in-law was productive in under 90 seconds.

Writesonic's dashboard has… a lot going on. Templates, agents, projects, brand voices, SEO tools, chat. Look, it's powerful — but the first-week learning curve is real. Budget two or three sessions before it clicks.

Winner: QuillBot. Not close.

The Rewriting Engines Themselves

This is where specs matter. QuillBot's paraphraser exposes two independent controls: mode (which changes the rewriting objective) and the Synonym slider (which changes lexical substitution aggressiveness). That's a 9 × 4 matrix — 36 possible transformation profiles from one input.

Writesonic gives you tone presets and Brand Voice. Fewer knobs, sure, but Brand Voice operates at the document level, which QuillBot flat-out can't do. Need 40 articles that all sound like the same writer? Writesonic wins. Need one paragraph to sound like a different writer? QuillBot wins.

Winner: split. Sentence-level → QuillBot. Document-level → Writesonic.

AI Detection and "Humanizing" — the part everyone lies about

Here's the deal. Neither tool reliably beats modern AI detectors, and anyone claiming otherwise is selling something.

In my eleven-run test, QuillBot's Humanizer + Creative mode + Synonym level 4 dropped detector confidence meaningfully on two of three detectors — but the output picked up awkward synonym choices ("utilize" where "use" belonged, that kind of thing). Writesonic's Brand Voice output scored better on readability while scoring worse on detection evasion.

My hot take: chasing detector scores is a losing arms race, and honestly, you'll produce worse content doing it. Detectors themselves have a well-documented false-positive problem on ESL writing — one Stanford study found non-native English essays got flagged as AI-generated over half the time. So you can "fail" a detector with writing you did entirely by hand. Use these tools to make text better, not to make it undetectable. If you genuinely need a detection audit, run Originality Ai as a separate check rather than trusting either vendor's built-in scorer.

Winner: QuillBot, narrowly, with an asterisk the size of a house.

Integrations and API

Writesonic runs away with this one. Documented REST API, Zapier, WordPress publishing, Surfer SEO, Semrush, Ahrefs, Google Search Console. You can wire it into a real pipeline and forget about it.

QuillBot? Chrome extension, a Word add-in, and desktop apps for macOS and Windows. Great for humans. Terrible for automation — there's no general-purpose public API at the individual tier, and I don't think that's an oversight so much as a deliberate positioning choice.

Winner: Writesonic.

Price vs. What You Get Back

At roughly $100/year, QuillBot Premium is one of the better value-per-dollar buys in this whole category. Writesonic's Lite tier starts near double that annually, and the tiers you actually want (Standard and up) run $79–$199/month.

But value depends on output. If Writesonic saves an agency 20 hours a month, $79 is trivial — that's four bucks an hour. If you're a grad student rewriting a lit review, $79/month is absurd.

Winner: QuillBot for individuals, Writesonic for teams.

When Something Breaks

QuillBot: email plus a solid help center. Response times in my experience ran 24–48 hours. No live chat on standard Premium.

Writesonic: live chat on paid plans, faster on higher tiers, plus onboarding calls at Professional and above. The community Slack is genuinely active, which is rarer than it sounds.

Winner: Writesonic.

On Your Phone

QuillBot ships native iOS and Android apps, plus a keyboard extension that rewrites inline in any app. It's genuinely useful on a phone — I've fixed emails on the subway with it.

Writesonic is web-first. The mobile browser experience works, technically, but it's cramped. You won't be running SEO audits from a train.

Winner: QuillBot.

Security and Compliance

Both encrypt in transit and at rest. Writesonic offers SSO, custom data retention, and enterprise agreements at the top tier — the things a procurement team will actually ask about. QuillBot has standard privacy controls and states it doesn't sell user content, but its compliance documentation is noticeably thinner.

If you're pasting client-confidential material, read both DPAs. Seriously. (Yes, all of it. I know. Do it anyway.)

Winner: Writesonic, on enterprise readiness.


Photo by Matheus Bertelli on Pexels

Pros and Cons, No Padding

QuillBot

Pros

  • Best-in-class paraphrasing granularity (9 modes × 4 synonym levels)
  • Free tier is genuinely usable, not a demo in disguise
  • ~$8.33/mo annual is hard to beat
  • Chrome extension + native mobile apps
  • Fast — sub-2-second inline rewrites

Cons

  • Can't generate content from scratch
  • Aggressive synonym settings produce odd word choices
  • No real API for automation
  • Plagiarism checker capped at ~20 pages/month
  • Thin enterprise compliance story

Writesonic

Pros

  • Full article generation with live SERP data
  • Brand Voice keeps 100 articles consistent
  • Real API + Zapier + WordPress publishing
  • Live chat support
  • SEO tooling that competes with dedicated platforms

Cons

  • Expensive at the tiers you'd actually use
  • Steep first-week learning curve
  • Rewriting is shallow compared to QuillBot
  • Credit systems have changed repeatedly (budget for surprises)
  • No native mobile app

Who Should Buy QuillBot?

Pick QuillBot if you're a student or academic — the citation generator plus Academic mode plus plagiarism checking is a complete workflow for under $100/year. That's less than most textbooks.

Get it if you're an ESL writer. Fluency mode is the single best tool I've found for making technically-correct-but-stiff English read naturally, and I don't say that lightly.

It's also the obvious call for freelancers cleaning up AI drafts. You already have the text. You need it to stop sounding like a model. That's exactly the job QuillBot was built for, and it's the clearest verdict in the whole QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026 comparison.

And if you're budget-constrained? The free tier alone beats most paid competitors. Fun fact: a lot of people never upgrade, and for casual use they're not wrong to skip it.

Grab it here: Quillbot

Who Should Buy Writesonic?

Choose Writesonic if you're running a content operation, not a document. Twenty-plus articles a month, multiple writers, a publishing calendar — that's the shape of the problem it solves.

Go with it if SEO is the actual point. The Search Console and Semrush integrations mean your content decisions come from real ranking data instead of vibes. Pair it with Surfer Seo if you want on-page optimization at the same depth.

It's the right pick if you need automation, too. The API and Zapier support let you build a pipeline; QuillBot can't do that at the individual tier, full stop.

And obviously — agencies managing client brand voices at scale.

In the QuillBot vs Writesonic for rewriting and humanizing AI content 2026 decision, Writesonic wins whenever "how much" matters more than "how precise."

Start here: Writesonic

The Verdict After Eleven Runs

For rewriting and humanizing specifically — the literal thing this keyword asks about — QuillBot wins. It's more precise, dramatically cheaper, faster, and it gives you actual control knobs instead of a single "make it human" button. At roughly $8.33/month annually, it's close to a no-brainer for individuals.

For producing content at scale where rewriting is one step of ten, Writesonic wins, and it isn't particularly close either. QuillBot simply doesn't play in that space.

The uncomfortable truth after eleven test runs? Neither one turns bad AI content into good human content. They transform surface text. Structure, argument, specificity, and genuine expertise — those still come from you. The best output I got across all eleven runs wasn't QuillBot's or Writesonic's. It was QuillBot's Fluency pass followed by me rewriting two paragraphs by hand, which took about six minutes and beat every automated variant.

My actual recommendation: buy Quillbot annual. If you later find yourself publishing more than 20 pieces a month, add Writesonic on top. They stack better than they substitute. If neither fits, Wordtune sits between them on price, and Jasper is the enterprise-brand-voice alternative to Writesonic.

You Might Also Like

  • QuillBot vs Hypotenuse AI for Content Editing and Rewriting 2026: An Honest, Numbers-First Comparison
  • Hypotenuse AI vs Jasper for Ecommerce Product Content 2026: An Honest, Data-Backed Comparison
  • Best AI Writing Tools for YouTube Scripts and Video Content 2026
  • Best AI Writing Tools for Students and Academic Writing 2026: 7 Picks Tested and Ranked
  • Frase Honest Review 2026 — Pros and Cons for SEO Content Briefs

FAQ

Q: Can QuillBot or Writesonic actually make AI content undetectable?
No. Be skeptical of anyone who says yes.

Q: Is QuillBot's free plan enough for casual use?
For occasional rewriting, yeah. The 125-word cap per paraphrase is the main friction — you'll end up pasting in chunks, which gets old around the fifth one. Grammar checking is unlimited and free, though, which is a better deal than it sounds. If you're rewriting daily, the annual Premium plan pays for itself in about a month of saved irritation.

Q: Which is better value for a solo blogger?
QuillBot at ~$100/year, unless you need articles generated from scratch. If you're writing your own drafts and just want them polished, Writesonic's Standard tier at ~$79/month is money you don't need to spend.

Q: Does Writesonic have a paraphrasing tool like QuillBot's?
It has rewrite and tone-adjustment features, but they're shallower — fewer modes, no synonym-aggression control, and less variation across regenerations. Three usable variants versus nine, in my testing. If paraphrasing is your core need, that gap decides the whole comparison on its own.

Q: Can I use both together?
Yes, and honestly that's what I'd do. Generate the draft in Writesonic, then run the problem paragraphs through QuillBot's Fluency or Creative mode. Runs about $180/year combined at entry tiers.

Q: Do either of them offer refunds?
QuillBot has historically offered a short money-back window on Premium — typically a few days, so don't dawdle. Writesonic's policy varies by plan and has changed more than once. Check current terms at checkout instead of assuming.

Q: Which one handles non-English content better?
QuillBot, again. It paraphrases across 20+ languages and translates across 45+. Writesonic generates in 25+ languages but its SEO tooling is clearly strongest in English.

Last updated: August 6, 2026. Pricing and feature sets change frequently — verify current tiers on each vendor's site before purchasing. Some links above are affiliate links; they don't change what I'd recommend, and the eleven test runs happened either way.
